title: Watching Migration From My Rooftop
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Every year in late autumn, thousands of birds pass directly above our city on their way south, though most people never even glance upward to notice.
Narrator: [honestly] I only started paying attention after my neighbor, an elderly man who has watched this migration for decades, invited me onto his rooftop one evening.
Narrator: [curious] I asked him how he even noticed birds so far above the noise and lights of the city, since I had genuinely never seen them before.
Narrator: [reflective] He said that once you learn their calls, you start hearing them even when you can't see them clearly against the darkening sky.
Narrator: [with feeling] That first evening, we counted over two hundred birds within just one hour, moving in loose formations toward some destination I couldn't fully imagine.

Narrator: [thoughtful] He explained that certain species travel thousands of kilometers each year, navigating partly by stars, even though scientists still don't fully understand every method they use.
Narrator: [amazed] I found that genuinely humbling, that a creature weighing almost nothing could cross entire countries using instincts we can barely explain with our advanced technology.
Narrator: [gently] He told me that if the city lights grew brighter every year, fewer birds would successfully complete their journey, since artificial light disorients their navigation badly.
Narrator: [concerned] As a result, he now turns off unnecessary lights during peak migration weeks, and he has convinced several neighbors to do the same small thing.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I asked whether such a tiny gesture actually mattered, given how enormous the city's overall light pollution remains despite his efforts.
Narrator: [warmly] He said even though he alone cannot fix the whole problem, doing nothing simply guarantees the outcome he fears, so he does what little he can regardless.
Narrator: [reflective] That answer stayed with me longer than the birds themselves did, honestly, because I recognized the same excuse in my own life about larger problems.
Narrator: [peacefully] Now, every autumn evening, I climb up to that same rooftop, watch quietly, and switch off my apartment lights before the birds pass overhead.
